module_title: Glass and Glazing for Windows and Doors

lessons.title: Types of Glass Used in Africa: Clear, Tinted, and Tempered
lessons.body:
In Africa, the three most common types of glass for windows and doors are clear, tinted, and tempered. Clear glass is the cheapest and most basic. It lets in maximum light but offers no heat or UV protection. In hot climates, clear glass can make rooms unbearably hot, so many builders use tinted glass instead. Tinted glass has a metallic coating or body tint that reduces solar heat gain and glare. Common tints are bronze, grey, and green. Bronze and grey are popular in West and East Africa for their heat rejection. Tinted glass costs about 20-30% more than clear but can cut cooling costs.

Tempered glass is heat-treated to be 4-5 times stronger than ordinary glass. When it breaks, it shatters into small, blunt pieces instead of sharp shards, making it much safer. In many African countries, building codes require tempered glass for doors, low windows (below 500mm from floor), and any glass that people might walk into. Tempered glass cannot be cut or drilled after tempering, so all fabrication must be done before the tempering process. It costs roughly double the price of clear glass.

For most residential windows in Africa, 4mm or 5mm clear or tinted glass is sufficient. For larger windows or areas with high wind loads, use 6mm. For doors and safety-critical areas, use 10mm or 12mm tempered glass. Always check local building regulations. When ordering, specify thickness, tint, and whether tempering is required. Ask your supplier for a certificate of conformity for tempered glass. Remember that laminated glass (two layers bonded with a plastic interlayer) is also used in some applications for security and sound insulation, but it is not as common as the three types above. Choose based on climate, budget, and safety needs.

lessons.title: Measuring and Cutting Glass Safely
lessons.body:
Measuring glass accurately is critical. Use a steel tape measure, not a cloth tape, because cloth stretches. Measure the opening in the aluminum frame where the glass will sit. For a window with glazing beads, measure the width and height between the rebates (the inner edges where the glass rests). Subtract 3-5mm from each dimension to allow for expansion and to make installation easier. For example, if the opening is 800mm wide, cut glass to 795-797mm. Always measure twice and write down the numbers. Use a pencil to mark the glass. Never use a pen; ink can be hard to remove.

Cutting glass requires a flat, clean surface. Use a glass cutter with a carbide wheel. Lubricate the wheel with a drop of light oil. Hold the cutter at a 90-degree angle to the glass and score a single, smooth line from edge to edge. Do not score twice over the same line; that dulls the wheel and creates a weak cut. After scoring, place a thin rod or pencil under the glass along the score line. Press down gently on both sides to snap the glass. For thick glass (6mm and above), you may need to tap the underside of the score line with the ball end of the cutter to help the break run.

Safety is paramount. Always wear safety glasses, gloves, and long sleeves. Glass shards are razor-sharp. Work in a well-ventilated area. Never cut glass near children or pets. After cutting, smooth the sharp edges with a fine file or a sharpening stone. For tempered glass, you cannot cut it yourself; it must be ordered to size from a supplier. If you must cut laminated glass, you need to cut both sides and use a solvent to soften the plastic interlayer. In Africa, many small workshops use manual glass cutters; practice on scrap pieces first. Always dispose of glass waste in a designated bin, never in regular trash.

lessons.title: Installing Glass with Glazing Beads
lessons.body:
Glazing beads are the strips that hold the glass in the aluminum frame. They can be made of aluminum, PVC, or rubber. The most common in Africa are aluminum beads with a rubber gasket. To install glass, first ensure the frame is clean and free of debris. Place the rubber gasket (also called glazing rubber) along the inside of the frame where the glass will rest. The gasket provides a cushion and a watertight seal. Cut the gasket at a 45-degree angle at corners for a neat fit. Push the glass into the frame, ensuring it sits evenly on the gasket. Do not force it; if it doesn't fit, check your measurements.

Next, install the glazing beads. Start with the longest sides. Snap the bead into the groove on the frame, using a rubber mallet to tap it gently into place. Work from one end to the other. The bead should sit flush against the glass. If the bead is too tight, do not hammer it; you may break the glass. Instead, check that the glass is centered and the gasket is not bunched up. For aluminum beads, you may need to use a bead clip or screw to secure them. In many African windows, beads are held by friction alone, but for larger windows, use stainless steel screws to prevent corrosion.

After installing all beads, check for gaps. Run your finger along the bead; it should feel smooth and tight. If there are gaps, water can leak in. You can apply a small bead of silicone sealant along the joint between the glass and the bead, but only if the gasket is not sufficient. For casement windows, ensure the glass does not interfere with the opening mechanism. For sliding windows, make sure the glass does not rub against the track. Test the window by opening and closing it. If everything is correct, the glass should be secure and rattle-free. Always wear gloves when handling glass and beads.

lessons.title: Using Rubber and Silicone Seals
lessons.body:
Rubber and silicone seals are essential to keep water, dust, and air out of your windows and doors. Rubber seals, also called gaskets or weatherstrips, are usually made of EPDM (ethylene propylene diene monomer) rubber, which resists UV, ozone, and temperature extremes. They come in various profiles: U-channel, wedge, and bulb. For glazing, a U-channel gasket is common. It fits around the glass edge and then into the aluminum frame. Silicone sealant is a caulk-like material that cures into a flexible rubber. It is used to fill gaps and create a watertight seal. In Africa, silicone is widely available in cartridges and comes in clear, black, white, and bronze.

When using rubber seals, cut them slightly longer than needed, then compress them into the frame. Never stretch rubber seals; they will shrink back and leave gaps. For corners, miter cut the rubber at 45 degrees and join with a drop of superglue or a special rubber adhesive. Ensure the rubber is seated fully in the groove. If the rubber is damaged, replace it; do not try to patch it. For silicone, first clean the surfaces with a cloth and alcohol to remove dust and oil. Apply a continuous bead of silicone along the joint. Use a caulking gun and cut the nozzle at a 45-degree angle to the size of the gap. Smooth the silicone with a wet finger or a plastic spatula. Do not use too much; excess silicone looks messy and can attract dirt.

Silicone takes 24 hours to cure. Do not touch or expose to water during this time. In hot climates, silicone can skin over quickly, so work in sections. For sliding windows, apply silicone along the track where the glass meets the frame, but do not block the drainage holes. For casement windows, seal around the perimeter of the glass after installing the beads. Remember that silicone is not a substitute for proper gaskets; it is a secondary seal. Always use neutral-cure silicone for aluminum, as acetic-cure (vinegar smell) can corrode the aluminum. Check seals annually and replace any that are cracked or peeling.

lessons.title: Handling and Transporting Glass Without Breakage
lessons.body:
Glass is fragile and expensive. In Africa, where roads can be rough, transporting glass without breakage requires planning. Always carry glass vertically, never flat. When glass is flat, it can bend and crack under its own weight. Use an A-frame rack or a wooden crate with slots. If you don't have a rack, lean the glass against a solid surface at a slight angle (about 10-15 degrees from vertical) and secure it with straps. Pad the glass with cardboard, foam, or blankets. Never let glass touch glass directly; the vibration can cause scratches or breakage. Place a soft material between panes.

When lifting glass, wear gloves with good grip. Lift with two people for anything larger than 1 square meter. Hold the glass by the edges, not the face. Never lift glass by the corners; it can twist and break. Carry glass vertically with the bottom edge supported. When setting glass down, place it on a clean, flat surface with padding. Do not set it on concrete or gravel. In a vehicle, place the glass behind the seats or in the bed, secured so it cannot slide. Avoid potholes and speed bumps if possible. If you must transport in a pickup, use a wooden frame and tie it down with ropes, but not too tight. Use rubber pads under the ropes.

For long distances, consider having glass cut and tempered at a local supplier near the job site to reduce transport. If you must transport tempered glass, remember it cannot be cut, so any breakage means a total loss. Always carry a spare piece if the budget allows. In rainy season, cover glass with a tarp to prevent water spots. When unloading, have one person guide the glass while another supports it. Never drop glass, even from a small height. Store glass in a dry, secure area on site, away from traffic. Use a glass rack with felt-lined slots. If glass is stored outside, keep it off the ground and covered to prevent damage from debris and weather.

lessons.title: Glazing Sliding and Casement Windows
lessons.body:
Glazing a sliding window requires attention to the track and rollers. First, remove the sliding panel from the frame. Lay it flat on a padded surface. The glass is held in the panel by glazing beads, usually on the inside. Remove the old beads with a putty knife or a flat screwdriver. Clean the frame and check the rollers. Replace any worn rollers. Cut the new glass to size, allowing 3-5mm clearance. Install the rubber gasket around the glass edge, then place the glass into the panel. Reinstall the beads, starting with the long sides. Tap them gently with a rubber mallet. Apply silicone sealant along the bead edges for a watertight seal. Do not seal the drainage holes at the bottom of the panel. Reinstall the panel into the track and adjust the rollers so the panel slides smoothly and locks properly.

For casement windows, the glass is held in the sash, which opens outward or inward. Remove the sash from the frame by unscrewing the hinges. Lay the sash flat. Remove the old beads and glass. Clean the sash. Cut new glass to fit, again allowing 3-5mm clearance. Install the rubber gasket, then the glass, then the beads. For casement windows, the glass is usually held by beads on the inside, but some designs have beads on the outside. Check your specific window. After glazing, apply silicone sealant around the glass on the inside. Reattach the sash to the frame. Check that the window opens and closes freely. Adjust the hinges if needed. For both types, ensure the glass does not come into contact with any metal parts; the rubber gasket should separate them. Test for leaks by spraying water on the window from outside. If water enters, reapply silicone. Always wear safety glasses when glazing. In Africa, many sliding windows use 4mm or 5mm glass, while casement windows often use 6mm for better wind resistance. Always follow the manufacturer's instructions for your specific window system.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Glass and Glazing for Windows and Doors

In African aluminium fabrication, glazing is where profit is won or lost. A window that leaves your workshop with a chipped edge, a leaking seal, or the wrong glass thickness will cost you a return visit, a replacement pane, and the reputation that brings the next contract. This practical reference pulls together the field-tested numbers, methods, and materials that fabricators from Lagos to Nairobi to Johannesburg use daily. Treat it as your bench manual: keep it open while you cut, seal, and install.

Why Glazing Specification Matters in African Markets

Most African construction operates under a mix of national codes and imported standards. South Africa enforces SANS 10400-N (glazing) and SANS 10137; Kenya references KS ISO 20492 for insulating glass; Nigeriaâs building code leans on BS 6262; and across the continent, European and Chinese profile systems dominate. The practical consequence is that a fabricator must know the glass thickness, edge condition, and glazing method that satisfy the clientâs engineer, the local authority, and the wind and thermal loads on site.

Business-first thinking means standardising on a small number of glass types and thicknesses that cover 80% of jobs, then ordering cut-to-size from a reliable processor. Every extra millimetre of glass is paid for twice â once at purchase, and again in the frame, bead, and gasket sizes you must stock.

Glass Types and Where They Pay Off

Clear float glass (4â6 mm) is the workhorse for residential windows in mild climates. It is cheap, widely available, and easy to cut. Tinted glass (bronze, grey, green, blue) reduces solar heat gain and glare â a strong selling point in hot, sunny markets such as Ghana, Senegal, and northern Nigeria, where cooling load is a real operating cost for the building owner. Tempered (toughened) glass is required for doors, full-height panels, and any location subject to human impact; it must be cut and processed before tempering, so order final sizes from the processor.

Table 1. Common glass types and typical African application
Glass type Typical thickness Best application Relative cost
Clear float 4, 5, 6 mm Residential windows, louvre frames Low
Tinted float 4, 6 mm Sun-facing faÃ§ades, offices, hotels Lowâmedium
Tempered clear 6, 8, 10 mm Doors, shopfronts, balustrades Mediumâhigh
Laminated safety 6.38, 8.38 mm Overhead glazing, security windows High
Low-E / reflective 6 mm High-end commercial, hot climates High

Source: Thickness and application guidance compiled from BS 6262-4 and SANS 10400-N; cost bands are indicative of West, East, and Southern African supplier pricing.

Measuring, Cutting, and Handling Without Breakage

Measure the rebate, not the frame opening. For dry glazing, subtract the gasket compression allowance â typically 2â3 mm per side for rubber gaskets â so the glass sits without stress. For wet glazing with silicone, allow 3â5 mm clearance. Always measure width and height at three points (top, middle, bottom) and use the smallest dimension; African frames are rarely perfectly square after transport and installation.

Cutting float glass is a scored-and-broken operation: clean the surface, apply a thin film of light oil, score once with steady pressure, and break over a felt-covered batten. Tempered and laminated glass cannot be cut on site â they must be ordered to final size. Edge quality is critical: a chipped or shelled edge becomes a crack initiation point under thermal movement.

â  SAFETY WARNING â CUTTING AND HANDLING GLASS

Always wear cut-resistant gloves, safety glasses, and closed shoes when handling glass. Never carry a pane flat against your body or under your arm; carry it vertically, edge-protected, with two people for panes above 1 mÂ². Store glass on edge in a rack, never flat on the ground. Dispose of offcuts immediately â a 200 mm sliver in a walkway causes serious lacerations. In hot African workshops, sweat reduces grip: use suction lifters or vacuum cups for panes above 6 mm. First aid for a cut: apply pressure, irrigate, and seek medical attention for deep wounds.

Installing Glass with Glazing Beads

Dry glazing with beads is the dominant method for aluminium systems because it is fast, clean, and allows glass replacement without cutting out cured silicone. The sequence is: fit the bottom and side gaskets, seat the glass on setting blocks (two per pane, positioned at quarter points), fit the remaining gaskets, then snap or screw the glazing bead into the frame. Beads must be cut with a 45Â° mitre at corners and a 2 mm expansion gap at the ends to avoid buckling in heat.

Wet glazing with silicone is used where watertightness is critical â coastal installations, high-rise faÃ§ades, and areas with driving rain. Use a neutral-cure silicone compatible with the frame finish; acetic-cure silicone can corrode some coated aluminium and attack PVB interlayers in laminated glass.

Table 2. Glazing method selection guide
Method Seal type Best for Replacement ease
Dry glazing (bead + gasket) EPDM or silicone gasket Residential, casement, sliding windows High â remove bead
Wet glazing (silicone) Neutral-cure silicone Coastal, high-rise, curtain wall Low â cut out sealant
Hybrid (gasket + silicone bead) Gasket + silicone High wind/rain zones Medium
Structural silicone glazing Structural silicone Commercial faÃ§ades Low â specialist

Source: Method classification based on BS 6262-4 and SANS 10137 glazing practice; replacement ease assessed from typical African fabrication workshop experience.

Rubber and Silicone Seals

EPDM rubber gaskets are the default for dry glazing: UV-stable, cheap, and available in standard profile shapes. Silicone gaskets cost more but last longer in intense UV and high temperature â worth specifying for coastal and desert projects. Silicone sealant (neutral cure) is the wet-glazing standard; apply a continuous bead, tool it within 10 minutes, and allow 24 hours before water testing. Never mix sealant brands on one joint â adhesion failure is the most common cause of leaks in African installations.

Glazing Sliding and Casement Windows

Sliding windows need the glass to sit in a rebate deep enough to resist wind uplift and to allow the sash to slide without binding. Set the glass on two setting blocks at quarter points, and ensure the bottom track has drainage slots clear of sealant. Casement windows are more sensitive to racking: the glass must be centred so the sash closes against the gasket evenly. Check the diagonal measurements before glazing â a sash out of square will crack glass when the stay is tightened.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Confirm glass type, thickness, and edge condition against the engineerâs specification and local code (SANS 10400-N, BS 6262, KS ISO 20492).
  • Measure rebate width and height at three points; use the smallest dimension and deduct gasket allowance (2â3 mm per side dry, 3â5 mm wet).
  • Inspect every pane for chips, scratches, and shelled edges before installation â reject damaged glass.
  • Use setting blocks at quarter points; never let glass rest directly on the frame or fixings.
  • Cut beads with 45Â° mitres and a 2 mm expansion gap; seal mitres with a small dab of silicone.
  • Use neutral-cure silicone only; never mix brands or use acetic-cure on coated aluminium.
  • Water-test sliding and casement units before handover; check drainage slots are clear.
  • Record glass batch, supplier, and installation date for warranty traceability.

Further Reading

  • South African Bureau of Standards (SABS) â SANS 10400-N and SANS 10137 glazing standards
  • Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) â KS ISO 20492 glass in buildings
  • BSI â BS 6262-4 Code of practice for glazing for buildings
  • National Glass Association (NGA) â Glazing best practice guides
  • African Glass Federation â regional fabrication and safety resources

quiz.q: Which type of glass is heat-treated to be 4-5 times stronger and breaks into small blunt pieces?
quiz.explanation: Tempered glass is heat-treated for strength and safety, breaking into small blunt pieces.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of tinted glass in African climates?
options: A) It is cheaper than clear glass
B) It reduces solar heat gain and glare
C) It is stronger than tempered glass
D) It can be cut after tempering
quiz.explanation: Tinted glass reduces solar heat gain and glare, making it popular in hot climates.

quiz.q: Why should you not cut tempered glass?
options: B) It will shatter into small pieces
C) It is already cut to size
D) It is coated with a special film
quiz.explanation: Tempered glass cannot be cut because it will shatter into small pieces if any edge is damaged.

quiz.q: What is the recommended clearance when cutting glass for a window opening?
quiz.explanation: A clearance of 3-5mm allows for expansion and easier installation.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for measuring glass accurately?
quiz.explanation: A steel tape does not stretch, ensuring accurate measurements.

quiz.q: What should you do after scoring glass with a cutter?
options: A) Score again over the same line
B) Tap the glass with a hammer
C) Place a rod under the score and press down
D) Heat the glass with a torch
quiz.explanation: Placing a rod under the score and pressing down snaps the glass along the score line.

quiz.q: Why should you wear gloves when cutting glass?
options: A) To keep the glass clean
B) To protect from sharp edges
quiz.explanation: Gloves protect your hands from sharp glass edges and shards.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of glazing beads?
options: B) To hold the glass in the frame
D) To make the window open
quiz.explanation: Glazing beads secure the glass in the aluminum frame.

quiz.q: Which material is commonly used for glazing beads in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Aluminum beads are common due to their durability and resistance to corrosion.

quiz.q: How should you cut rubber gasket at corners?
quiz.explanation: A 45-degree miter cut allows for a neat corner joint.

quiz.q: What should you do if the glazing bead is too tight?
options: B) Check glass centering and gasket
quiz.explanation: A tight bead often means the glass is off-center or the gasket is bunched.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of silicone sealant in glazing?
options: B) To provide a watertight seal
C) To make the glass stronger
quiz.explanation: Silicone sealant fills gaps and prevents water and air infiltration.

quiz.q: Which type of rubber is commonly used for window seals?
quiz.explanation: EPDM rubber resists UV, ozone, and temperature extremes, making it ideal for windows.

quiz.q: Why should you not stretch rubber seals during installation?
options: B) They will shrink back and leave gaps
quiz.explanation: Stretched rubber seals shrink back over time, creating gaps.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to apply silicone sealant?
options: A) Apply a thick bead and leave it
B) Apply a continuous bead and smooth it
quiz.explanation: A continuous bead smoothed with a wet finger ensures a proper seal.

quiz.q: How long does silicone sealant take to cure?
quiz.explanation: Silicone typically takes 24 hours to fully cure.

quiz.q: Why is neutral-cure silicone preferred for aluminum?
options: C) It does not corrode aluminum
quiz.explanation: Acetic-cure silicone can corrode aluminum; neutral-cure is safe.

quiz.q: How should glass be transported?
quiz.explanation: Glass should be transported vertically to prevent bending and breakage.

quiz.q: What is the maximum angle from vertical for leaning glass?
quiz.explanation: Leaning glass at 10-15 degrees from vertical is safe and stable.

quiz.q: Why should you not let glass touch glass during transport?
quiz.explanation: Vibration can cause glass-to-glass contact, leading to scratches or breakage.

quiz.q: How many people should lift a glass pane larger than 1 square meter?
quiz.explanation: Two people are needed to safely lift larger glass panes.

quiz.q: Where should you store glass on a job site?
options: B) In a dry, secure rack
quiz.explanation: A dry, secure rack protects glass from damage and weather.

quiz.q: What is the first step in glazing a sliding window?
quiz.explanation: The sliding panel must be removed to access the glass and beads.

quiz.q: What should you check before reinstalling a sliding panel?
options: A) The color of the glass
B) The condition of the rollers
D) The weight of the panel
quiz.explanation: Worn rollers should be replaced for smooth operation.

quiz.q: For casement windows, where are glazing beads usually located?
quiz.explanation: Most casement windows have beads on the inside, but check your specific design.

quiz.q: What should you do after glazing a casement window?
options: B) Test for leaks with water
quiz.explanation: Spraying water tests the seal and reveals any leaks.

quiz.q: Which glass thickness is common for sliding windows in Africa?
quiz.explanation: 4mm or 5mm glass is standard for residential sliding windows.

quiz.q: What is a key safety rule when glazing?
quiz.explanation: Safety glasses protect your eyes from flying glass fragments.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid blocking drainage holes when sealing?
options: B) They allow water to escape
C) They make the window stronger
quiz.explanation: Drainage holes prevent water buildup in the frame.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to dispose of glass waste?
options: B) In a designated glass bin
quiz.explanation: Glass waste should be disposed of safely in a designated bin to prevent injury.
